About the Medical Reading event

Medical Reading is a Health Science event in the HOSA secondary division. Format: testing.

Companion analysis for the five HOSA 2026–27 assigned books. Full books were not available for authoring, so this course does not supply chapter summaries, invented book facts or a replacement for reading. Publisher and author pages establish the reading map; all practice passages are explicitly original fiction, and background sections draw on public health and research sources rather than the books. Read each complete assigned book and verify details in your own copy. The official test allocates ten questions to each book; local FRQs are learning checkpoints, not official HOSA scoring.

Medical Reading lessons

Crisis Averted · prevention and public systems

Analyze evidence and preparedness alongside the assigned Rivers book.

  1. Crisis Averted: read prevention claims and invisible outcomes 20 min

    When an outbreak does not grow, did prevention work, was the threat smaller than expected, or did several things change together? Reading a prevention narrative requires examining what happened and what comparison…

  2. Crisis Averted: institutions, communication and preparedness 20 min

    A response can contain sound scientific advice and still fail if nobody knows who will carry it out. This lesson studies the connection between evidence, responsibilities and public communication through an original…

Everything Is Tuberculosis · science, history and inequality

TB background from CDC and WHO, braided narratives and arguments about why a curable disease persists.

  1. Everything Is Tuberculosis: braided narratives of science, history and a patient 25 min

    Some nonfiction moves between one person’s story, centuries of history and the biology of a microbe. A strong reader keeps the strands separate enough to answer precise questions, yet connects them enough to understand…

  2. Everything Is Tuberculosis: why a curable disease persists 25 min

    If a disease can be cured, why does it still kill so many people? Answering requires reading an argument that links biology, poverty, cost and history—and evaluating which links the author supports with evidence.

Fragmented · continuity and coordination

Handoffs, missing information and evaluating a clinician-author’s argument for change.

  1. Fragmented: handoffs, missing information and continuity of care 25 min

    A test result that no one owns, a medication list that differs between two hospitals, a specialist who never hears back—each is small, but together they describe what it means for care to be fragmented.

  2. Fragmented: evaluating a physician’s argument for change 25 min

    A clinician-author who has seen the same failure many times may write with urgency. Reading well means taking that experience seriously while still testing each claim, recognizing counterarguments and judging which…

The Next Patient · emergency medicine

Triage, time and sequence, diagnostic uncertainty and the people behind emergency care.

  1. The Next Patient: reading emergency medicine under time pressure 25 min

    Emergency departments run on triage, interruptions and decisions made with incomplete information. Narratives set there move quickly between patients and often compress hours into pages. Reading them well means tracking…

  2. The Next Patient: uncertainty, judgment and the people behind emergency care 25 min

    Emergency clinicians decide quickly with incomplete information, and some decisions turn out to be wrong. Narratives about this work explore judgment, error, teamwork and the personal cost of the job. A careful reader…

Grit · evidence, practice and putting it together

Evaluating a psychological concept, study strategies and cross-book synthesis for the essay tiebreaker.

  1. Grit: defining, measuring and testing a psychological idea 25 min

    Popular psychology books often introduce a concept with a memorable name. Before accepting that the concept explains success, a careful reader asks how it is defined, how it is measured and what the research does and…

  2. Grit and the whole reading list: practice, purpose and exam preparation 25 min

Each test is an original, full-length simulation of the HOSA Round One written test, written to run slightly harder than the real thing. Every answer comes with an explanation and a reference.

Sample Medical Reading questions

1. Accepting a diagnosis before it has been fully verified is called:

  1. Diagnostic momentum reversal
  2. Triage
  3. Premature closure
  4. Overshadowing
Show answer

C. Premature closure

Premature closure stops the search for other explanations too early.

2. Which action is an example of a nonpharmaceutical intervention during an outbreak?

  1. Giving a new antiviral drug
  2. Isolation and better ventilation
  3. Developing a new vaccine
  4. Prescribing antibiotics early
Show answer

B. Isolation and better ventilation

Nonpharmaceutical interventions slow spread without medicines, through measures such as isolation, masking, ventilation and distancing.

3. Which communication principle helps public health officials keep trust during an evolving outbreak?

  1. Never admitting uncertainty
  2. Releasing information only after the crisis ends
  3. Using only technical jargon
  4. Being transparent about what is known and unknown
Show answer

D. Being transparent about what is known and unknown

Honest, timely communication about uncertainty supports trust when guidance has to change.
